name: News story: correlation as cause
description: A news story that finds a real pattern in survey data and jumps straight to declaring one thing causes the other.
trap: Correlation treated as causation, self-reported data
subject: Data and graphs
generation_instructions:
Write a short news story about the topic that reports a survey and then argues for a policy.

The chart must contain the trap:
- Use kind "scatter" with 14 to 22 points that slope, but not perfectly.
- Mark 3 or 4 points as outlier: true, placed clearly against the trend, so a student can find cases that break the pattern.
- Start y_min above 0 so the slope looks steeper than it is.
- The footnote must reveal that people estimated their own numbers rather than anything being measured.
- Set annotation to a short note about the axis or the sample.

The body should state the pattern as proof of cause and recommend an action. Do not mention other explanations, and do not explain the flaw where a student can see it. Put the explanation only in thinking_trap.

The transcript should be four short lines where a participant admits they guessed their own number.

offline_draft.title: Is {topic} Hurting Test Scores?
offline_draft.subject: Data and graphs
offline_draft.blurb: The school paper surveyed 200 students and says {topic} is hurting math scores.
offline_draft.intro: This story about {topic} ran in the school newspaper last week.
offline_draft.body: {topic} is hurting student learning. We asked 200 students at Lincoln Middle School how many hours a day they spend on it. Students who said more than 4 hours got an average of {low}% on the math final. Students who said less than 1 hour got an average of {high}%. That is a {gap} point difference. The graph makes the pattern clear. Our school should cut back on {topic} during the school day so that test scores go up.
offline_draft.opening_prompt: Read the story and look at the graph. What is one question you would ask before you believe it? You can highlight a sentence or click a part of the graph to show what you mean.
offline_draft.thinking_trap: A pattern between two things does not tell you which one causes the other, or whether something else causes both. Students who study less might both do more of this and score lower, so {topic} could be a symptom rather than a cause. The hours are also guesses, not measurements, and several students high on the scale still scored well.
offline_draft.chart_alt: A dot graph with hours across the bottom and math scores up the side. The dots slope downward, but several students high on the scale still scored above 85.

chart.title: Reported hours and math final score
chart.footnote: 200 students. Hours were guessed by each student, not measured.

transcript.text: Reporter: We asked students how many hours a day they spend on it.
Student: Maybe two hours? I never actually counted.
Reporter: We handed out the survey in one class period.
Principal: These numbers show we need to cut back on {topic}.
